matched_endpoints.assay_desc: NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2 is a biochemical, single-readout assay that uses extracted gene-proteins from insect cells in a cell-free assay. Measurements were taken 0.5 hour after chemical dosing in a 96-well plate.
matched_endpoints.assay_source_desc: NovaScreen, part of PerkinElmer, a human and environmental health company, provides a large diverse suite of cell-free binding and biochemical assays.
matched_endpoints.assay_component_desc: NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2 is one of one assay component(s) measured or calculated from the NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2 assay. It is designed to make measurements of enzyme activity, a form of enzyme reporter, as detected with fluorescence intensity signals by Fluorescence technology.
matched_endpoints.assay_component_target_desc: Changes to fluorescence intensity signals produced from an enzymatic reaction [Reaction:CEC + NADPH --> 7-hydroxy-3-cyanocoumarin (CHC) + NADP+] involving the key substrate [7-ethoxy-3-cyanocoumarin (CEC)] are indicative of changes in enzyme function and kinetics for the human cytochrome P450, family 1, subfamily A, polypeptide 2 [GeneSymbol:CYP1A2 | GeneID:1544 | Uniprot_SwissProt_Accession:P05177].
matched_endpoints.assay_component_endpoint_desc:
Data from the assay component NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2 was analyzed into 1 assay endpoint. This assay endpoint, NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2, was analyzed in the positive analysis fitting direction relative to Acetonitrile as the negative control and baseline of activity. 
Using a type of enzyme reporter, loss-of-signal activity can be used to understand changes in the enzymatic activity as they relate to the gene CYP1A2. 
Furthermore, this assay endpoint can be referred to as a primary readout, because this assay has produced multiple assay endpoints where this one serves a enzymatic activity function. 
To generalize the intended target to other relatable targets, this assay endpoint is annotated to the cyp intended target family, where the subfamily is xenobiotic metabolism.
matched_endpoints.assay_title: NovaScreen (NVS) CYP450-related Enzyme Activity (ADME) Assay for human CYP1A2
matched_endpoints.assay_objectives: The NVS biochemical assay portfolio includes enzymatic and binding assays for specified G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), cytochrome P450 mono-oxygenase enzymes (CYPs), kinases, phosphatases, proteases, histone deacetylases (HDACs), nuclear receptors, ion channels, and transporters. The assays were selected from a commercial ‘NovaScreen’ panel (NVS) for preclinical drug development based on published evidence linking assay targets to pathways of toxicity, cell signaling and xenobiotic metabolism. Some assays were simple component systems (e.g., purified recombinant mammalian protein expressed in bacterial or insect systems) and others multi-component (e.g., membrane fractions from tissue homogenates or soluble fractions from cultured human cell lines). Both human and non-human assay targets were investigated to allow cross-species comparison of orthologous assay results. The chemical library screened provides an excellent prototype for initial exploration of HTS technologies intended to probe a broad range of interactions relevant to pathways of biological activity and potential toxicity.
matched_endpoints.assay_throughput: All assays for the biochemical high throughput screening were initially run in duplicate at a single concentration (10 uM for CYP450 assays and 25 uM for all others). Actives and a subset of negatives followed a secondary screen to re-test chemical-assay pairs in 8-point concentration series from 0.023 to 50 uM (or 0.009–20 uM for CYPs).
matched_endpoints.scientific_principles: Understanding how singular or combinatorial perturbations of molecular targets propagate to in vivo toxicities is a key challenge. The classification of chemicals by their relative activities on cell-free biochemical and pharmacological assays can reveal a number of susceptible targets that play important roles in pathways that may lead to key events in toxicity.
matched_endpoints.biological_responses: NVS is a biochemical HTS (high-throughput screening) that employs profiled cell and tissue extracts using semi-automated biochemical and pharmacological methodologies to evaluate a subset of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), CYP450 enzymes (CYPs), kinases, phosphatases, proteases, HDACs, nuclear receptors, ion channels, and transporters. The observed effects of the chemicals on the cell-free assays are mostly inhibition, but in some cases activation. The half-maximal activity concentration (AC50) revealed both known and novel targets in signaling and metabolic pathways.
matched_endpoints.analytical_description: Raw data for each replicate assay plate was internally normalized and corrected to scale the data between 0% inhibition (DMSO control) and 100% (positive controls). Data were scaled such that a value of 100% represents full inhibition relative to the maximal effect of the reference compound. To characterize scale, data spread near the center and the tails was measured. Median absolute deviation (MAD) was computed as median of the absolute value of the difference between x and  xmed (median |x-xmed|), where x is the parameter data element and xmed is the parameter median. Unlike standard deviation, this measure does not square the distance from the median, so it is less affected by extremes in the tail and can provide a reasonably stable estimate of spread for data with extreme values in the tails. For single-point screening, values in the −20% to +20% range of inhibition were considered noise. Negative inhibition in the primary screen was considered on a case by case basis for technical artifact (radioligand binding assays, chemical interference with the measurement technology), enhanced ligand binding (assays run in antagonist mode), or stimulation due to a direct effect (enzymes) or coupling to another protein in the fraction.
matched_endpoints.basic_procedures: Binding assays used specific radioligands (tritiated, iodinated) with non-radioactive competitive displacement ligands in agonist or antagonist protocols (as indicated) and various reference compounds and inhibitors to titrate specific binding to receptors and transporters. Most enzyme assays (CYPs, kinases, phosphatases, proteases, HDACs) used recombinant protein and specific substrates (fluorescence mostly, some colorimetric and radioactive) and inhibitors, followed by a biochemical separation of substrate and product. All assays for the biochemical HTS were initially run in duplicate at a single concentration (10 uM for CYP450 assays and 25 uM for all others). Assay-chemical combinations meeting a pre-defined threshold (e.g., 30% inhibition and other criteria defined below) were then run in singleton concentration–response format with maximum concentration of 20 uM for CYPs and 50 uM for all others. Each assay was run with positive and negative controls, and concurrent controls on every plate. The follow-up (secondary) screen tested active chemical-pairs in concentration series, as well as a few additional assays not tested in the primary screen, some selected negative inactives, and several cases re-run in the concentration series for confirmatory purposes. Negative chemical-assay combinations were selected to include, for instance, all chemicals within a particular class, chemicals previously reported to target particular pathways, and some that showed negative inhibition.
matched_endpoints.experimental_system: Details on individual assays, catalogue numbers, quality assurance methods and literature references can be found at http://www.caliperls.com/products/contract-research/. The assay panel was distributed as follows: 77 G-protein coupled receptor binding assays; 32 CYP450-related enzyme activities (ADME) that included 30 distinct assay targets plus 2 redundant assays with observed activation (activator mode); 132 enzymatic assays (ENZ) that included 72 kinases (13 activator mode), 22 phosphatases (3 activator mode), 15 proteases, 6 HDACs (1 activator), 3 cholinesterases and 14 other enzyme activities; 18 nuclear receptor binding assays (NR); 20 ion channel (IC) and ligand-gated ion channel (LGIC) activities; 9 transporter proteins (TR), 2 mitochondrial pore proteins (MP) and 2 other receptor types (OR) for a total of 292 assays. Most assays are human (194) or rat (66) targets, in addition to 10 bovine, 10 guinea pig, 3 mouse, 3 rodent (rat/mouse), 2 sheep, 2 boar and 2 rabbit targets.
matched_endpoints.xenobiotic_biotransformation: Xenobiotic biotransformation potential has not been characterized. Although some of these assays may use tissue extracts, metabolism typically does not occur in a cell-free system.
matched_endpoints.proprietary_elements: The NVS assays were developed and run by Caliper Discovery Alliances and Services (Hanover, MD).

matched_endpoints.assay_component_endpoint_desc:
Data from the assay component NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2 was analyzed into 1 assay endpoint. This assay endpoint, NVS_ADME_hCYP1A2, was analyzed in the positive analysis fitting direction relative to Acetonitrile as the negative control and baseline of activity. 
Using a type of enzyme reporter, loss-of-signal activity can be used to understand changes in the enzymatic activity as they relate to the gene CYP1A2. 
Furthermore, this assay endpoint can be referred to as a primary readout, because this assay has produced multiple assay endpoints where this one serves a enzymatic activity function. 
To generalize the intended target to other relatable targets, this assay endpoint is annotated to the cyp intended target family, where the subfamily is xenobiotic metabolism.
